# Preface
- this document considers two different versions of lhs data 
-- one with 100 fixed cycles (designated as **v1**)
-- the other with dynamic convergence (convergence_threshold at 0.01) which is designated as **v2**
- Further all of the data displayed below is only considering M (mixed) debates which constitute a mix of pro and anti reduction agents (a future version to be run next week - form 25/5/26 onwards will introduce better segmentation and cross comparison of H and M debates)
- All analyses where data is not labelled in **v1** or **v2** is run with **v1** (which biases the interpretation as each debate is forced to run until it reaches 100 cycles)
- use_distinct_agents: __TRUE__ (each agent has the same base parameter value but has a standard deviation associated with each parameter) / __FALSE__ (all agents in that debate have the same parameter value -> assumes agents are all the same)

# Empirical data discovery

## Empirical Cross comparisons
- primary attitude change (8-17% of scale range) occurred between t0-t1 (sd almost twice the size of the mean change) 
- mean attitude change from t1->t2 is around 3-4% (with the exception of homogeneous which sways in the negative direction) left for simulation during debate (statistically indistinguishable from spontaneous drift in control)

## Linear Regression for Cohen's D
- std estimate represents cohen's d --> (-0.034, p value = 0.655), no significance of population on mean change from t1->t2

## Opinion Change T1 to T2
- small positive change in heterogeneous group / slight negative change in homogeneous group -> could be due to it being all anti_reduction so they create echo chambers leaning in the wrong direction (further away from pro_reduction of meat consumption)

## Combined Bar Chart
- Represents mean change across 3 time periods
- change from t1 -> t2 is minimal --> weak empirical signal with insignificant cohen's d implies difficulty in simulating opinion change given that it is assumed that deliberation creates social influence in this experiment

# PCC and PRCC (Pearson (Partial) Correlation Coefficients)
## Description of Data in LHS
- v1: 100 fixed cycles 6-5-26
- v2: dynamic convergence 4-5-26

## PCC for combined versions
- most parameters show weak relationships with mae (normal given unoptimized LHS)
- convergence rate shows strongest negative PCC with opinion_variance -> faster convergence reduces opinion spread
- confidence_threshold_sd notable negative relationship with opinion_variance in **v1**, distinct agents in confidence_threshold reduces variance

## PRCC for combined versions
- convergence_rate strengthens against opinion-variance (survives controlling for other parameters)
- confidence_threshold_sd relationship strengthens
- mae remains largely insensitive to all parameters (random parameters cannot beat the baseline)
- convergence_cycle in **v2** shows moderative negative PRCC with mae
- OVERALL: convergence_rate and opinion_variance have strongest relationship

# Model Performance Comparisons
## MAE by model type and version bar chart
+ __FALSE__ & __TRUE__ labels denote speaking mode (exposure driven influence)
- Dynamic convergence systematically outperforms fixed cycle implementation across all conditions
- None of the models in speaking mode TRUE/FALSE has a lower mean MAE than the no_change condition (agents are initiated and do nothing --> no change)

## Model Performance Across Versions
- Reasonably large overlap in error bars for bipolarization across both versions, however mean mae is lower in the speaking mode (TRUE) condition --> speaking_mode does have a positive impact on reducing mean mae

## MAE by model type and version bar chart (RED)
+ __FALSE__ & __TRUE__ labels denote speaking mode (exposure driven influence)
- here the "best" model is the lowest mae model in that panel (e.g., consensus, clustering, no_change, bipolarization)
- clustering consistently has the smallest delta (best performance compared with no_change)
- dynamic convergence outperforms fixed cycles in all conditions
- CAVEAT: pre-GA unoptimized lhs values, rankings may shift after GA runs

## ABM vs OLS comparison table
- Only the instance of Mixed debate 12 outperforms the ols mae (taken as a baseline)
- As only mixed debates appear in this table it can be assumed that they are for a large part heterogeneous (i.e. composed of pro and anti consumption reductiona agents)
- Delta_mae: positive (abm is worse), negative (abm is better)

## Model type comparison with no_change
- No model beats the no_change mean_mae (we still ahve slightly too much error but the dynamic converging **v2** seems to come close under clustering and consensus models with speaking mode)
- Worst two models are consensus and bipolarization in the **v1** with 100 fixed cycles

# Behavioral Effects
## Debate Composition on Mean MAE (table)
- Biased because data is filtered by Mixed debates
- No_change with speaking_mode ( __FALSE__ still outperforms all other models)
- Consensus with speaking_mode ( __TRUE__ ) and distinct_agents ( __FALSE__ and __TRUE__ ) shows some promise

## Debate Composition on Prediction Error
- Biased again because of only representing M debates
- __FALSE__ and __TRUE__ labels represent speaking mode
- when speaking mode is true bipolarization has a slight edge over the other models but still does not beat no-change
- the tail of bipolarization in both speaking_mode conditions implies a larger amount of interactions between agents which gives rise to a greater standard deviation of mae (ligns up with bipolarization dynamics)

## Speaking Mode and Debate Composition on MAE impact
- Speaking mode __TRUE__ globally has a lower mean mae than __FALSE__ but does not beat no_change
- n column: represents the amount of interactions (broadcasts) that occur (for reference: one interaction could be agent 1 speaking with agents 2,3,4,5 in one cycle) - the number here is slightly inflated due to the nature of how these interactions are collected and the fact there are multiple interactions in one cycle (i.e. one agent broadcasts to multiple others)

# Robustness
## Using Distinct Agents
- across all three models (excluding no_change) introducing distinct agents increases the mae compared with non_distinct agents
- caveat is that the samples sizes are large with __TRUE__, makes sense given it is a binary parameter with unequal representation in latin hypercube sampling

# interpretation
On average models achieve 52% directional accuracry, while producing higher MAE than no change
- suggests that dynamics introduce noise that slightly exceeds predictive signal at aggregate level
- the global average masks substantial debate level heterogeneity
-- homogeneous debates consistently achieve ~80% directional accuracry -> mechanics are well specified for opinion proximate groups but poorly calibrated for high variance heterogeneous debates

## Overall
1. global performance is modest but above chance
2. homogeneous conditions drive the positive signal
3. pro reduction agents and heterogeneous debates are systematic failure modes

# ABM vs OLS Performance
- biased because we are only showing the results of **v1**
- significantly worse (than the ols which is the baseline), forcing the debates to run the full 100 cycles introduces nosie that can degrade predictive accuracry

  mutate(sender_is_pro = sender_opinion > 0.5) %>%

# interpretation
1. models beat direcitonal baseline ~80% in homogeneous conditions
2. saturation is 6x higher in heterogeneous vs homogeneous
3. pro reduction agenets show systematic wrong-direction bias

# pro interpretation
- pro leaning speakers move anti agents roughly 2x more than anti leaning speakers
- bipolarization shows largest absolute cross position delta: shows highest wrong direction rates (may be moving anti agents more but not always in the right direction)
- This suggests cross-position influence is operative within the bounded confidence framework, though the absolute magnitude remains small — reflecting the attenuating effect of inertia and retention discount mechanics on entrenched positions (Festinger 1957, Nowak & Vallacher 1998).

## Network Plots for Homogeneous Debates
- theorized impact of how the influence network can be represented when new experiments are re-run
+ Legend description
- node size (out_strength): total wegithed influence an agent exerts on others across all interactions (larger nodes are more influential speakers in the debate)
- Node color (pro_reduction): agents position on pro or anti reduction, absent here given that these are 
- Node shape (agent_is_saturated): circles (FALSE) agents whos opinion remained within bounds throughout debate, triangles (TRUE) agents whos opinion reached opinion saturation (their opinion hit the scale boundary and could no longer move in one direction, this is a bipolarization specific phenomenon)
- Edge width (edge_weight): cumulative strength of influence between two agents, how much one agent's opinion shifted another's across all of their interactions, thicker edges indicate stronger dyadic influence relationships
- arrows: direction of influence flow between agents

## Homogeneous plot (homogeneous debates, only anti reduction agents)
- all agents are anti-reduction
- network structure is relatively sparse and linear (chains of influence)
- opinions in homogeneous groups operate through sequential cascades rather than reinforcing loops

## Heterogeneous plot (heterogeneous debates, both pro and anti agents)
- network is more dense, bipolarization has tighter clusters with heavier edges (cross-position influence is stronger, pro speakers move anti agents ~2x more)
- saturation is more frequent

```{r, debate-classifier, echo = FALSE}
# variance threshold classifier
df_classifier <- df_lhs %>%
  group_by(selected_debate_id, debate_label) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_var = mean(initial_variance),
    mean_mae = mean(mae),
    best_model = model_type[which.min(mae)],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(predicted_type = ifelse(mean_var < 0.01,
                                 "consensus", "bipolarization"))

df_classifier %>%
  mutate(correct = best_model == predicted_type) %>%
  summarize(accuracy = mean(correct))

```

## debate classifier
- LHS results suggest that initial variance plays a significant role in the predictor of model suitability.
- one could use a preliminary classifier for GA runs to check which model would work "best" for a specific debate
- debates with var < 0.01 are predicted to favor consensus, dynamics while high-variance favor bipolarization

-- next stage set-up
- could classify debate by initial variance, then apply GA optimization for that predicted model
- preliminary classifier is too simple, variance is not the only predictor
